planting.note: Set out bare-root divisions or liners in spring once soil has warmed, giving the narrow upright clumps full sun and good drainage.

directions: This switchgrass selection grows as a slender, strictly upright column of mid-green blades that resists flopping even in wind and rain. Silvery plumes rise above the foliage from midsummer into fall, adding airy texture and winter interest if left standing. Plant in full sun in average to lean soil and let the clump dry somewhat between waterings once established, since it tolerates drought and heat with little fuss. Its narrow profile makes it useful as a vertical accent or screen without the sprawl of older switchgrass types.

planting.note: Install divisions or liners in spring in full sun; this compact switchgrass holds a tidier, bouquet-like shape than taller selections.

directions: A compact switchgrass that stays shorter and denser than most, with smoke-rose flower sprays appearing from mid-summer and lasting into fall. It works well massed as a groundcover-scale accent or combined with later-blooming perennials where its soft coloring can set off brighter flowers. Grow in full sun and let it dry down between waterings, as it handles heat and drought easily once rooted in. Deer tend to leave it alone, and it needs minimal feeding or grooming through the season.

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; avoid overwatering, since soggy crowns on this selection are prone to rot issues.

directions: This switchgrass earns its name from the rounded, ball-like form the foliage takes on once it flowers, resembling a tumbleweed caught mid-roll. The compact habit stands up well to wind and heavy rain without splaying open the way many switchgrasses do. Give it full sun, lean watering, and good drainage to avoid crown rot, and expect reliable fall color and seedhead interest. It is a good fit for mixed borders or mass plantings where a rounded textural accent is wanted.

planting.note: Give this tall, columnar grass plenty of room in full sun; it is sterile and non-seeding, so it will not self-sow into surrounding beds.

directions: A tall, narrow silver grass with horizontally banded foliage that keeps its upright, columnar shape without staking or flopping. Feathery seed heads appear in early fall, adding another season of interest well after most perennials have finished. Because this selection is sterile, it will not produce the volunteer seedlings that make some older miscanthus cultivars a nuisance. Place it in full sun with room to reach its full mature height, and expect good rust resistance and minimal pest problems.

planting.note: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun; this selection breaks bud roughly two weeks ahead of typical catmint for earlier color.

directions: This catmint forms a low, wide mound that opens its blue-purple flowers noticeably earlier in the season than standard catmint types, stretching bloom from late spring through fall. The flowers are also larger than average for the genus, giving a showier display at a compact scale. Grow in full sun with light, infrequent watering once roots are established, since it handles heat and dry spells well. Its aromatic foliage is generally left alone by deer and rabbits while still drawing in bees and butterflies.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil; shear lightly after the first flush to encourage repeat bloom.

directions: A larger-growing catmint that sends up full, plume-like flower spikes well above the minty, gray-green foliage from spring into summer. The upright habit gives it more vertical presence than mounding catmint types, making it useful toward the middle of a border. It thrives in full sun with regular moisture during establishment, tapering to more drought tolerance once mature. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the blooms readily, and deer tend to avoid the aromatic leaves.

planting.note: Transplant into full sun in well-drained soil; deadhead spent spikes to push additional bloom cycles.

directions: This dwarf sage packs intensely colored, dark fuchsia-pink flower spikes with near-black calyxes onto a tight, compact plant well suited to the front of a border or a container. The deep foliage color and small stature set it apart from older, taller salvia selections. Grow in full sun with regular moisture and divide every few years to keep the clump vigorous. Pollinators visit the spikes readily, and the plant tends to be left alone by deer.

planting.note: Transplant into full sun in well-drained soil; shear back after the first bloom flush to encourage rebloom.

directions: A low, rounded sage that bears soft sky-blue flower spikes over healthy dark green foliage for most of late spring and summer. It grows a bit larger and spreads a bit wider than its Bumbleberry sibling, giving it more presence as a mid-border filler. Full sun and steady moisture keep the mound dense and floriferous, while occasional deadheading extends the bloom window. The flowers draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, and the plant is rarely troubled by deer.

planting.note: Transplant into full sun in sharply drained soil; this selection reblooms without needing a cold vernalization period.

directions: This compact pink dianthus forms a tidy, silvery-foliaged mound studded with bicolor flowers from early spring clear through fall, a notably long bloom window for the genus. Because it flowers without a chilling requirement, growers and gardeners alike get color earlier in the season than with older pink types. Plant in full sun in soil that drains quickly, since it tolerates occasional wet weather better than many pinks but still prefers not to sit wet. It is fragrant, drought tolerant once settled in, and generally ignored by deer.
